title: Treaty of Paris (1783)
description: Agreement ending the American Revolutionary War
wiki_lead:
The Treaty of Paris, signed by representatives of King George III of Great Britain and representatives of the United States on September 3, 1783, officially ended the War of American Independence and recognized the Thirteen Colonies, which had been part of colonial British America, to be free, sovereign, and independent unified states. It forms one treaty out of many that are collectively named the "Peace of Paris".
The treaty set the boundaries between British North America, later called Canada, and the United States, on lines the British labeled as "exceedingly generous", although exact boundary definitions in the far-northwest and to the south continued to be subject to some controversy. Details included fishing rights and restoration of property and prisoners of war.
Only Article 1 of the treaty, which acknowledges the United States' existence as free, sovereign, and independent states, remains in force.

Agreement

Peace negotiations began in Paris in April 1782, following the fall of Prime Minister Frederick North's government on 20 March, in the wake of British defeat at Yorktown in the U.S. War for Independence at the hands of the Continental Army, the French Royal Army, and the French Royal Navy.  The negotiations continued through the summer of 1782. Representing the United States were Benjamin Franklin, John Jay, Henry Laurens, and John Adams. Representing the Kingdom of Great Britain and King George III were David Hartley and Richard Oswald.
The treaty was drafted on November 30, 1782, and signed at the Hôtel d'York at present-day 56 Rue Jacob in Paris on September 3, 1783, by Adams, Franklin, Jay, and Hartley.
In September 1782, French Foreign Minister Vergennes proposed a solution to deadlocked negotiations between the United States and the British, which was rejected by the United States. France was exhausted by the war, and all parties sought peace, except for Spain, which insisted on continuing the Revolutionary War until it could capture Gibraltar from the British. Vergennes developed treaty terms under which Spain would forego holding Gibraltar and the United States would be granted independence, but it would be confined to the area east of the Appalachian Mountains. Britain would keep the area north of the Ohio River, which was part of the Province of Quebec. In the area south of that would be an independent Indian barrier state, under Spanish control.
The American delegation perceived that they could obtain a better treaty in negotiating directly with the British in London. John Jay promptly told the British that he was willing to negotiate directly with them and to bypass France and Spain, and British Prime Minister Lord Shelburne agreed. In charge of the British negotiations, some of which took place in his study at Lansdowne House, now a bar in the Lansdowne Club, Shelburne now saw a chance to split the United States from France and to establish the new nation as a valuable economic partner. grok_lead: The Treaty of Paris of 1783, formally known as the Definitive Treaty of Peace, was a bilateral agreement signed on September 3, 1783, in Paris between commissioners of the United States of America and Great Britain that concluded the American Revolutionary War and acknowledged the independence of the thirteen former British colonies as a sovereign nation. The American commissionersâ Benjamin Franklin (Minister Plenipotentiary to France), John Adams, and John Jay (both with plenipotentiary powers)âengaged in negotiations with British representative David Hartley under the ministry of the Earl of Shelburne. Article 1 explicitly stated that "the said States hereby solemnly publish and declare, That the said United States are of right, and ought to be, free sovereign and Independent States," thereby establishing the legal basis for American nationhood free from British allegiance or territorial claims. Key territorial provisions in Articles 2 and 3 delimited the new republic's boundaries, extending from the Atlantic Ocean westward to the Mississippi River, northward to the Great Lakes, and southward to the 31st parallel near Spanish Florida, granting the United States control over vast western lands previously claimed by Britain. Additional clauses addressed navigation rights on the Mississippi River for both parties, guaranteed American fishing privileges off Newfoundland and the Grand Bank, and committed to the restoration of confiscated property and pre-war debts, though enforcement of the latter proved contentious in practice. The treaty's ratification by the Confederation Congress on January 14, 1784, marked the formal cessation of hostilities, though separate agreements under the broader Peace of Paris resolved conflicts with Britain's allies France and Spain. Its generous territorial concessions to the United States, exceeding even the Continental Congress's initial aspirations, stemmed from Britain's strategic prioritization of dividing its American adversaries and weakening French influence post-Yorktown defeat, while American diplomats exploited divisions in the British government to negotiate independently of their French allies. Despite subsequent disputes over implementation, such as British retention of frontier forts and Loyalist compensation, the treaty laid the foundational framework for the expansion of the United States and reshaped North American geopolitics by ceding imperial ambitions in the continent's interior.
